title: Ganges treaty: with 24 days left, Dhaka says it is ready to negotiate and is waiting for Delhi
dek: Bangladesh's water minister has written to his Indian counterpart asking for talks, and officials in Dhaka are floating an interim extension. India has not announced a date for negotiations.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Bangladesh says it has finished preparing for talks on the Ganges water-sharing treaty and is waiting for India to come to the table, with 24 days left before the 1996 agreement that divides the river's dry-season flow at Farakka in Murshidabad expires on 12 December. Its Water Resources Minister, Shahiduddin Chowdhury Anee, has recently written to his Indian counterpart asking for formal negotiations to begin without delay, according to reports published in Dhaka on Wednesday.

India has not announced a date for negotiations or for any interim arrangement. A Bangladeshi foreign ministry official said experts were suggesting a temporary extension of the treaty, but that "India also has to agree" and that the decision would have to be taken at the political level, according to reports. The Indian High Commission in Dhaka had not commented, reports said.

## What Dhaka says

Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, an adviser to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman who heads Bangladesh's technical committee on the treaty, said in a written statement that Bangladesh had completed its preparations and hoped India would start formal talks before the deadline, according to reports. He said the region that depends on the Ganges, known as the Padma in Bangladesh, covers about a third of the country and is home to more than five crore people.

Dhaka first told New Delhi in June that it had set up a high-level technical committee and asked India to name its own team, and repeated the request in August, according to reports. Mr Anee has said Bangladesh wants a new treaty with a "guarantee clause" securing its share in the leanest weeks, rather than a simple renewal.

Humayun Kabir, a former Bangladeshi ambassador, said a meeting between the two prime ministers could settle on one of several options: renewing the treaty for another full term, a short extension, or a one- or two-year extension while it is reviewed. "We have to have some kind of agreement as soon as possible before this one expires," he said, according to reports.

## India's position

The Ministry of External Affairs has said all river matters, "including Ganga", are handled through the Joint Rivers Commission, the body the two countries set up in 1972. At its briefing on 3 November, spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said there was no update on a meeting of the commission, and that India had invited Mr Rahman to visit. No visit has been announced.

India has been consulting its own states. West Bengal attended four meetings of an inter-ministerial review committee between October 2023 and March 2025, and Bihar attended four between August 2023 and May 2024, according to reports. West Bengal has asked for adequate dry-season flows down the Bhagirathi-Hooghly, which carries water to Kolkata and its port. In July, Parliament's Standing Committee on External Affairs urged the government to finish its review and start talks with Bangladesh without further delay.

## What is at stake for Bengal

The treaty, signed on 12 December 1996, sets a formula for sharing the water that reaches Farakka from 1 January to 31 May each year. In the driest weeks, between 11 March and 10 May, each country is guaranteed 35,000 cusecs in alternating ten-day periods. A joint committee measures the flow every day at Farakka and at Hardinge Bridge in Bangladesh. Article XII says it can be renewed only "on the basis of mutual consent"; there is no automatic extension.

If no arrangement is in place by 12 December, the dry season of 2027, which begins less than three weeks later, would be the first since 1996 without an agreed sharing rule or joint measurement of the river. For West Bengal, the treaty decides how much water India can send down the feeder canal into the Hooghly in those months; for Bangladesh it governs the flow into the Padma and the south-west of the country.

## What happens next

The treaty runs until the end of 12 December. Any extension, interim arrangement or new treaty needs both governments to agree. Neither side has announced a meeting of the Joint Rivers Commission or a summit before then.
